clinicalPearls: Muehrcke lines are paired transverse white bands running parallel to the lunula across the nail, classically separated by strips of normal pink nail.
They are an apparent leukonychia arising in the nail bed, not the plate, so the bands do not move distally as the nail grows and disappear when the nail bed is compressed or a tourniquet is applied.
The classic association is hypoalbuminaemia, particularly nephrotic syndrome, and the lines may resolve if the serum albumin normalises.
They are also described with chemotherapy, malnutrition, chronic liver disease and other systemic illnesses that lower albumin or disturb nail bed vasculature.
Because the abnormality is in the bed rather than the plate, blanching with pressure is a useful bedside test that distinguishes them from true leukonychia and from Mees lines.
Mees lines, by contrast, are true plate leukonychia that do migrate distally and are linked to arsenic and thallium poisoning and severe systemic insults.
Muehrcke lines are asymptomatic and are a clinical sign to investigate rather than a disease to treat.
They typically affect several nails symmetrically, most often the second, third and fourth fingers.
reference.pathophysiology: Muehrcke lines are a form of apparent leukonychia, meaning the whiteness originates in the nail bed rather than in the keratin of the nail plate. The prevailing explanation is a localised oedematous or vascular change in the nail bed, associated with hypoalbuminaemia, that alters the way light is transmitted through the normally translucent plate and produces the appearance of pale transverse bands. Because the plate itself is structurally normal, the bands remain fixed in position while the nail grows and vanish transiently when pressure empties the underlying vascular bed. When the provoking state, most commonly a low serum albumin, is corrected, the abnormal transmission of light resolves and the lines fade. This mechanism cleanly separates them from true leukonychia, in which the plate keratin is abnormal and the white mark migrates distally.
additionalInvestigations: Renal function and urinalysis for proteinuria/nephrotic syndrome
Blanch test with digital pressure to confirm bed origin
Review of recent chemotherapy or systemic illness
redFlags: Newly appearing lines in the context of unexplained weight loss or systemic illness
Associated heavy proteinuria or oedema suggesting nephrotic syndrome
Signs of decompensated liver disease alongside the nail changes
Coexisting features that might instead indicate Mees lines and heavy-metal exposure
reference.prognosis: Muehrcke lines are themselves benign and often reversible, fading when the underlying hypoalbuminaemia or systemic illness is corrected. Their significance lies in flagging the underlying disorder, whose prognosis they follow.
pitfalls: Confusing Muehrcke lines with Mees lines and missing heavy-metal poisoning, or vice versa
Failing to perform the blanch test that distinguishes bed-based from plate-based whiteness
Treating the nail sign rather than investigating the underlying cause
Assuming the lines will migrate out with the nail, which they do not
